Co-Editors’ Farewell

Susan Fabrick LCSW and Ruth Livingston PHD

Ruth Livingston

Email: sfabrick@aol.com

Email: ruthlivingstonphd@gmail.com

Ruth Livingston  

Ten Years! That’s how long Susan Fabrick and Ruth Livingston have been co-editors-in-chief of Contemporary Psychoanalysis.1

And what an astonishing time in history! We’ve watched the United States and the world change, including major shifts brought on by the 2016 presidential election, the #MeToo era, the COVID pandemic, the Black Lives Matter movement, the Supreme Court’s Dobbs decision revoking abortion (Roe vs. Wade), the rise of right-wing populism, and the 2024 presidential election (with all its twists and turns).

It’s been a challenge—a dance, really—to keep up, all the while tending to our mission to provide readers with a broad array of content from new and returning voices. In these 10 years, as before, the focus of Contemporary Psychoanalysis has been on publishing articles that highlight new perspectives on theoretical ideas and clinical work in this “impossible” profession. Especially in this decade’s turbulent times, we’ve also featured psychoanalytic reflections on current events and considered psychoanalytic history. Sadly, we’ve lost some giants in the interpersonal psychoanalytic world; we’ve honored them in our pages.

Below, some highlights of these 10 years of co-editor-ship, which have included several special issues and sections devoted to important developments and topics. (Much gratitude in this decade goes to the guest editors and panel organizers who chose authors and set the tone for many of these special issues/sections: Max Belkin, David Braucher, Rande Brown, Meredith Darcy, Sue Grand, Elizabeth Howell, Sheldon Itzkowitz, Lois Oppenheim, Jill, Salberg, Pascal Sauvayre, Sarah

Nina Jamshidnejad MA M.Sc.

Nina Jamshidnejad

Email: n.jamshidnejad@wawhite.org

Nina Jamshidnejad   Born, raised, and educated in Iran: B.A. (English Literature), M.A. (Cultural Studies), and M.Sc. (Psychology) where she has more than a decade of experience as a licensed individual and group psychoanalyst. She recently relocated to New York where she is currently a part of the Licensure Qualifying Program in Psychoanalysis at the William Alanson White Institute (WAWI). Ms. Jamshidnejad has also translated a number of psychological and psychoanalytic books, including Object Relations in the Life and Work of Melanie Klein (a collection of Melanie Klein’s papers translated to Farsi); Val Parker’s A Group-Analytic Exploration of the Sibling Matrix: How Siblings Shape Our Lives; and Behr and Hearst’s Group-Analytic Psychotherapy: A Meeting of Minds, among others, into Farsi.
identification with the aggressor, Sándor Ferenczi, Iran, Woman Life Freedom, hijab, political oppression

This article examines the complex relationship that Iranian women have with the compulsory hijab in Iran and the recent shift in their attitudes toward it. Using Sándor Ferenczi’s concept of “identification with the aggressor,” I explore how the imposition of the hijab, enforced by a repressive regime, led to an internalization of the aggressor’s values and beliefs. Through analyzing the phenomenon of identification with the aggressor that happens following traumatic events, the author argues that Iranian women internalized the regime’s power dynamics, resulting in a sense of fear, shame, and guilt associated with the abandonment of the hijab. The Woman, Life, Freedom movement, however, challenged this internalized oppression, sparking a collective shift toward defiance and liberation. Here, the author highlights the importance of understanding the dynamics of identification with the aggressor in the contexts of political oppression, and underscores the crucial role of resistance and truth-telling in dismantling internalized forms of control.

Psychic Self-Exile: The Infantile Parent and the Erased Child

Stephanie Lewin PHD

Stephanie Lewin

Email: stlewin@aol.com

Stephanie Lewin   Private practice in New York City, having received her doctorate in 2001 from the Gordon F. Derner School of Psychology. She has written a series of articles about transference work with schizoid patients, published in Contemporary Psychoanalysis and Psychoanalytic Dialogues.
infantile, schizoid, exiled-self, self-erasure, identification, reparation

This article proposes a connection between the infantile parent and the schizoid child. Infantile love is described as ruthless: envious, greedy and demanding. The author suggests that the schizoid child fends off the infantile parent’s “love” by disappearing: if the child cannot be seen, then she cannot be attacked. A case illustration is provided wherein a young woman, raised by an infantile mother, disappears via two unconscious self-states; a perpetually anxious erased-self, and a rageful, despairing exiled-self. Diffuse and uncertain, the erased-self was a fog that the infantile mother could not penetrate. Nonverbal and rageful, the exiled-self diminished her relationships. Both self-states cemented the young woman’s psychic disappearance—becoming an effective, if self-depriving, defense against the infantile mother’s threat. The author asserts that acknowledging the true threat of the infantile mother in the transference enabled the dyad to dispel the fog of the erased-self, and to integrate the exiled-self.

History Beyond Trauma: The Enduring Legacy of Davoine and Gaudillière

James Gorney PHD

James Gorney

E-mail: jegorney@comcast.net

James Gorney   Received his Doctorate from the University of Chicago. He completed a post-doctoral fellowship and went on to serve on the supervisory staff at the Austen Riggs Center. He is a graduate of the William Alanson White Psychoanalytic Institute and has taught at New York Hospital-Cornell, Duquesne, and the University of Tennessee. He is the author of various papers on innovations in psychoanalytic technique, Winnicott, Lacan, and self-psychology. He is the recipient of the Hans Strupp award for excellence in psychoanalytic education and the ISPS-US Bertram Karon Memorial award for psychoanalytic writing. Dr Gorney is currently in private practice in Knoxville, Tennessee.
trauma, psychosis, war psychiatry, Lacan, intergenerational transmission

History Beyond Trauma (2004) by Davoine and Gaudillière is a groundbreaking, creative contribution to the theory and treatment of trauma, madness, and psychosis. The authors’ profound understanding of extreme states, both in their genesis and implications for treatment, has been unjustly overlooked and neglected within mainstream psychoanalysis. This paper contributes an overview of the singular careers of Davoine and Gaudillière, and also provides a detailed explication of History Beyond Trauma. This masterwork substantiates how devastating pieces of individual, familial, or social history, when cut out of symbolic discourse, constitute traumatic experience. It is only through therapeutic witnessing that unformulated, unrepresented trauma can be inserted into the social link of a transformative human relationship. This healing process will be illustrated via vivid clinical examples drawn from diverse psychoanalytic perspectives. The insights of History Beyond Trauma will thus be demonstrated as relevant for a wide range of clinical practice.

Richard Gartner PHD

male sexual victimization, male sexual abuse, group therapy for sexually traumatized men, male sexual trauma, male sexual betrayal

Men sexually traumatized as boys or adults usually feel isolated and lonely. Nevertheless, they may be fearful of relationships, having felt betrayed when trust was broken during abuse and assault, often by a trusted other. Individual treatment can help heal these wounds. But this process may be accelerated in group therapy with other men having sexual abuse histories. The common feelings of isolation, shame, and de-masculinization may be repaired from having the lived experience of being with other men dealing with similar feelings. In this paper, members of a long-term therapy group for sexually abused men share their experience of how the group experience repaired their sense of self, agency, and masculinity. Key themes include: recognizing the experience as abusive; realizing they were not at fault; being in the company of other men and making connections with them; taking risks; feeling a sense of community and family; feeling changed; and transference to one another and the group leader.

The Splitting of the God Image

Robin Xu MD

Robin Xu

60 Littleton Road, Suite 203A, Parsippany NJ, 07054
Email: robinxumd@gmail.com

Robin Xu   Currently in private practice in Parsippany, New Jersey. He received a Bachelor’s Degree in Chemistry/Molecular Biology and Biochemistry from Rutgers University, and an M.D. from St. George’s University. In addition to his outpatient work, he is currently a fourth-year psychoanalytic candidate at the William Alanson White Institute of Psychiatry, Psychoanalysis and Psychology in New York City. His interests include psychoanalysis, mythology/religion, philosophy, and the interplay among these fields.
God, deconversion, theodicy, illusion, object relations, splitting

The decline of faith in Western civilization has removed one of the previously consistent pillars of meaning and comfort humanity has relied upon from its beginning. Many explanations have been postulated for this phenomenon, including economic factors, sociological changes, and scientific advances, among others. In this article, I suggest that a key factor in the increasing secularization of our society may involve the problem of evil in a world now dominated by science and technology. While theodicy, the reconciliation of an “all-good,” “omnipotent” deity with the existence of evil, has always been a challenge for believers, I aim to show how the need for theodicy can be a result of one’s God image being split along the same lines as one’s primary objects. I suggest that this split is increasingly hard to maintain in the context of our changing worldviews. My object relational analysis of the God image and its relation to the problem of evil will draw primarily on work by Freud, Ana-Maria Rizzuto, and Fairbairn. I propose that the segregation of the objectionable, evil elements of the human condition away from an all-good God, functioned as long as there were viable alternatives for these elements to be displaced onto. Now that this is increasingly not the case, a religion whose God image remains split becomes much less resilient to the realities of life, as compared to one whose God image is able to hold both the good and evil elements simultaneously.

Shame, frame, frame bend, ritual, spontaneity, relational-constructivist framework

Relational psychoanalysis encourages us to challenge traditional approaches, instead emphasizing a dialectical relationship between ritual and spontaneity. However, to some, relational freedom conflates an open attitude with unruly technique. In addition to the abundance of ritual provided by a customary frame, a coconstructed relational frame includes the option of moving beyond a generic version toward one more adapted to a particular patient’s needs. A frame bend that arises spontaneously from a shame-based impasse can be viewed as existing within the figure-ground relationship, between ritual and spontaneity, which upholds the dialectical constructivism underlying a relational framework.

containment, container/contained, ‘clinical’ vs. ‘psychosocial’ concepts, W.R. Bion, psychosocial methodology

This article critically retraces the passage of W.R. Bion’s concept of ‘containment’ from the clinic to the psychosocial domain. In doing so, it lays emphasis on the extent to which psychosocial applications of psychoanalytically derived concepts, such as containment, are fruitful. The central tension in any such transposition stems not only from the high level of complexity that characterizes the social, but also the extent to which such a transposition demands certain conceptual revisions, as well as careful methodological reflection. With these considerations in mind, this article explores the tension between, on one hand, ‘being true’ to the original conceptual and theoretical contours of containment, and, on the other hand, a concept of social containment that is capable of doing justice to the complexity and richness of social experience.

This paper examines the phenomenon of involuntary intrusive thinking, including thoughts and images involving aggressive and violent behavior. These uncensored intrusions emerge from all levels of awareness: unconscious fantasies, the preconscious, and the conscious. I propose that exploring intrusive thinking in analysis can serve as an opening for richer examination of a patient’s inner world, since intrusive thinking is often an indication of underlying conflict. The clinical narrative follows the path of an analytic dyad negotiating their way through the treacherous territory of toxic stress and transmission of both intergenerational and transgenerational trauma, from father to son. Central to the discussion is the pronounced transference–countertransference imbedded in the analysis from the onset, and the relational approach that ultimately eased the relationship between analyst and patient, and offered a path toward resolution.

freud, counterculture, adaptation, individuality, civilization and its discontents, lionel trilling

One of the fundamental challenges we face throughout our lives is that of pursuing our hopes, longings, and goals when the norms, beliefs, values, and ideals we have internalized from our culture thwart our desires. When we are stymied in pursuit of our wishes, we can feel discontented with our culture. While Sigmund Freud, in Civilization and its Discontents (1930), emphasized that the self must capitulate to the strictures of culture1 (Freud resisted the distinction between “culture” and “civilization”)—and cannot therefore achieve true happiness—knowledge we have gained (in evolutionary biology, attachment theory, and psychoanalysis) since Freud wrote his classic text provides a more sanguine and expansive vision of how we can feel more personally fulfilled while living in civilization.

Each of us, I propose, has an amicable and an adverse relationship with culture. We have an intrinsic desire to engage with culture and an equally intrinsic desire to disengage from culture. These desires correspond to our social self and our asocial self—the part of us that strives to be free from influence by external reality (Winnicott, 1963). Because of the double-edged nature of our relationship with culture, we are continually challenged to find ways to live with dual—at times dueling—longings. Negotiating this dual relationship and creating a viable balance between the two dimensions poses a major psychological challenge throughout our lives. It requires the capacity to quarrel with culture and use our discontent to create a fluid, versatile self that can traverse two realms of experience: being a part of culture and being apart from culture. Cultivating a dual relationship—in which engagement and disengagement with culture are vital—enables us to feel greater contentment.

The author examines Loewald’s developmental perspective on Oedipal development in the context of young adulthood, namely the act of parricide and all that it entails. Extending Loewald’s idea that parricide is a mutual act, the author further interpersonalizes this concept in looking at the various manifestations parricide may take as the young adult tries to commit the murder of parental authority. Particular attention is given to the obstacles that often stand in the way of parricide and how parent and the young adult navigate these obstacles both separately and together. The author places emphasis on development as an ongoing, lifelong, process and the importance of reparation between parent and young adult as they both seek to find ways to move generativity into the foreground such that it can facilitate the act of parricide.

Psychoanalysts working with patients who are dying must focus on the emotional and psychological conflicts faced by individuals dealing with terminal or life-altering illness. Who am I? This is a point of inquiry that confronts us all, as members of the human race. Locked in the deepest corridors of our minds are the ingredients, the elements, that inform who we believe ourselves to be, or long to become. All too frequently, though, particularly in the aftermath of psychological trauma, critical aspects of lived experience are rendered unavailable to us. They remain defensively hidden from conscious experience, although they actively, and consistently, exert influence upon our sense of selfhood. These observations hold relevance for our work with our patients, who seek our help in locating a more stable sense of self, one that feels less intrapsychically and interpersonally alienated. How do psychoanalysts help our patients find meaning in answer to their search? The answer rests in the fact that the conduct of psychoanalysis is, itself, an act of creativity. Like poets, for instance, psychoanalysts invite our patients into liminal, or potential spaces, where internalized, dissociated experiences, might be interrogated creatively. As is true of poetry, psychoanalysis has the capacity to draw patient and analyst alike into psychic interiors, where resides the complexity of our humanity—always dynamic, always yearning, always alive, even if as yet unknown. Psychoanalysis, as does poetry, cradles us into as yet unauthorized corridors, trespassing past sentinels of the mind standing guard against truths as yet unthought. It is an otherworldly interior that we enter, one constituted of the rhythms of pain, and loss, of rage, and of the love that poetic forms elicit. The experience transcends fantasy. It is, rather, more like being in a dream—one that, in the exquisite language of D. W. Winnicott (1971/2005), “ha[s] poetry in it, that is to say, layer upon layer of meaning related to past, present, and future, and to inner and outer, and always, fundamentally about [one’s]self” (p. 48). With two case presentations, the author discusses how psychoanalytic form and language, in concert with poetic form and language, can attenuate the power of rigid, dissociative boundaries, and guide our patients’ journey toward discovery and potential change.

Liminality is explicated for what it illuminates about the psychoanalytic setting, the dream-like, old-new photography of Maggie Taylor and its correspondence with the psychoanalytic project, and a persistent tension between finitude and the wish to be infinite that is inherent in the human condition. We regularly manage to dissociatively eschew curiosity to avoid the anxieties associated with encountering the new and the unfamiliar because we prefer to know what’s coming rather than to experience the unfamiliar as it comes. Psychoanalysis aspires to be a necessarily strange situation in which defenses against emergent experience can recede, allowing for potentially generative “losing” of what has been, while simultaneously encountering what might be next.

To be in a liminal space, physically, emotionally, or metaphorically means to be on the precipice of something new but not quite there yet. Until recently, the word liminal was mostly confined to academia. Its roots are in Latin, from “līmen,” meaning “threshold” or “doorstep.” In anthropology, it’s used to describe the middle part of a ritual or rite of passage. Anthropologist Arnold van Gennep (2019)1 first wrote about the concept of liminality when he developed the idea of the rites of passage. He defined them as sequential: preliminal rites (or rites of separation), liminal rites (or transition rites), and postliminal rites (or rites of incorporation). This transition theory argued that changes in people’s life stages follow such a pattern. Many of these changes look like they are endings—and they are to some degree–but they are really lines in the sand. British anthropologist Victor Turner’s 1967 book chapter Betwixt and Between2 describes the liminal phase of ritual as a departure from the ordinary rules of time, space, and social hierarchy, where people can experiment with their identity. The word has gone on to mean a time or place of transition, usually with eerie, nostalgic, or surreal connotations. Since the start of the pandemic, a niche genre of photography has grown in popularity called “liminal spaces.” It has captured the eeriness and isolation of pandemic life as a time or place of transition, a period marked by uncertainty.

The liminal is between two worlds—on the very edge of what it means to be human—where everything is stripped away from you; where you transcend this life, and experience something beyond it.

This article explores the liminality between life and death, suggests a collective longing to communicate with the departed, and addresses psycho-analysis’ struggle with the existential trauma of mortality. The author (LD) describes her attempt to communicate with someone who had died through her dreams. This is followed by a paranormal experience wherein the deceased person ‘visited’ her while she was awake in the form of a felt presence of an angry bird trying to attack her. body, psychoanalysis, trauma, intersectionality, somatic

The embodied impact of trauma complicates the work of helping our patients access more enlivened states of being. Like all trauma, the intersecting traumas of racism, misogyny, and sexual violence can lead to chronic autonomic nervous system dysregulation that forecloses the capacities for fantasy, imagination, and insight so central to the psychoanalytic process. Somatic approaches can be enlisted to support the patient in developing an “embodied observing ego” that tracks present moment bodily experiences signaling the presence of anxiety, defense, core affect, and trauma survival responses. As self-regulatory capacity increases, the patient is helped to consciously execute trauma survival responses which had previously been inhibited or truncated. This approach, informed by the work of Pierre Janet (1919/1925) and contemporary neurobiology and traumatology (e.g., Levine, 1997; T. Ogden, 2019), and by sensorimotor psychotherapy in particular (T. Ogden, 2019), allows patients to experience a previously inaccessible stage of “triumph,” and unlocks their capacities for meaning making and integration. I outline this embodied psychodynamic approach through clinical illustrations from my work with an Indian American woman grappling with the effects of racialized and gendered trauma.

intersex, transgender, bisexuality, queer theory, gender

This paper explores liminal sexual and gendered subjectivities and identities – in particular bisexuality, transgenderism, and intersexuality – with an attention to the intersections of race, culture, and class. It argues that the potential space of psychoanalysis should work to make room for forms of subjectivity that defy identity, and which often fall through the cracks of cultural intelligibility. It challenges psychoanalysts to tolerate ambiguity; to allow sexuality and gender to at once orient and disorient. It addresses the problem of identity itself, arguing that good psychoanalytic practice at once acknowledges the limitations of identity and accepts that its formation is critical to helping people make sense of their own complexity. It argues that queer theory should be a necessary part of psychoanalytic education. And finally, it offers numerous clinical examples, including an extended case study of a patient who struggles with the biological ambiguity of his sexed body and with the difficulty of finding the language to make sense of it.

Amiri Baraka, American poetry, suicidal fantasy, Hettie Jones, racial hatred

This article explores possible meanings of Amiri Baraka’s poem “For Hettie,” published in his first book, Preface to a Twenty Volume Suicide Note …. (1961). It grows out of my research on suicidal fantasy in American authorship and wonders what “For Hettie,” a poem about family and pregnancy, among other things, has to do with the suicidal fantasy evoked by the book title. Distinct from most interpretations of Amiri Baraka’s poetry, I draw on the interpersonal psychoanalytic clinical practice of asking questions about what’s literally happening in the poem. This leads to a new perspective on hatred in Baraka’s poetry where the object of hatred is more confused than decided and, thus, not clearly politically radical in the ways Baraka’s poems are generally considered to be. Moreover, the poem “For Hettie” is not often the subject of criticism or inquiry in Baraka scholarship. I suggest that this is because the poem brings together suicidal fantasy, pregnancy, interracial love, and hatred, foregrounding the importance of conceptualizing confusion as an important experience in reading poetry.

trauma, mutual transformation, ruptures, identity, healing

In this article, I use the witnessing of a tragic accident and the relationship formed between me, as a first responder, and the victim to describe how in psychoanalysis patients and analysts collide in what Apprey terms “pluperfect errands.” The use of these errands can be an ontological tool in the psychoanalytic relationship and have helped form my identity as a psychoanalyst. Drawing associative links between this story and the analytic dyad, this story travels in and out of tragedy, hopefulness, and repair, resulting in mutual trauma, transformation, and healing, much like what takes place between patient and analyst. I raise the following questions in this paper: Who in analysis is listening to whom? What forms the unique analytic identity? And how does therapy repair the ruptures of previous traumas for both patient and analyst? This paper addresses the inevitable personal and professional entanglements of analysts and details how our histories and haunts are recognized and processed with our patients.

The clinical implications of Winnicott’s transitional object theory are expanded to encompass all cases, rather than just cases in which patients suffer basic developmental deficits. This article explores the interplay of personal imagination with actual objects and people, in relation to clinical practice and problems in living. Good-enough integration in the transitional phase moves toward flexible and reciprocal relations between the inner and outer worlds that are at the core of wholesome psychosomatic vitality in development and everyday life. Problems in that integration are apparent in most difficulties in living. Since the transitional, potential space is crucial to this interplay of the inner imagination and the outer world, attention to its fluxes and flows will enrich the analytic process, whether as a primary focus or in enhancing other approaches.

William Alanson White, social reform, history of psychoanalysis, racism, interpersonal psychoanalysis

Although widely considered one of America's most prominent psychoanalysts and psychiatrists in his time—serving twice as president of the American Psychoanalytic Association (1915–6, 1927–8)—William Alanson White's revolutionary contributions to socio-cultural theory and his legacy of advancing broad societal and mental health reforms have largely been forgotten. Though he was the leading proponent of Freud in the United States, White rejected the evolving orthodoxy of newly formed American training institutes, advocating instead for an interdisciplinary perspective attentive to societal conditions. He produced the first English-language psychoanalytic textbook and journal, championed child labor laws, and wrote seminal work on psychiatric education, community mental health, and criminal reform. White struggled to improve conditions at the segregated St. Elizabeths Hospital and attempted, unsuccessfully, to racially integrate psychiatric training—progressive stances sharply at odds with prevailing attitudes during an era of Jim Crow, violent labor strife, and mass incarceration.

analyst’s otherness, transitional space, Sheldon Bach, subjective and objective self-awareness, enactments of “me” and “not-me, ” sadomasochistic organizations

There are some patients for whom otherness disrupts precarious experiences of personal coherence and stability. Analysts and patients are thus sorely challenged to find bridges between inside and outside, fantasy and reality, self and other, subjectivity and objectivity—the in-between spaces that give psychoanalysis its particular power. This article explores the clinical dilemmas in working with such patients who tend to present as either lost in subjective experience with little connection to externality, or as trapped in an objectified reality devoid of personal vitality. Winnicott’s conceptualization of transitional space, and Sheldon Bach’s elaboration of related capacities to move fluidly between states of subjective and objective self-awareness, are used to: 1) illuminate what’s missing in both presentations, and 2) describe the enactments that unfold between “me” and “not-me.” To the degree that its present, subjective experience is either disconnected from, or conflated with, externality. For patients without access to transitional space, its emergence will likely be from within these pathological organizations in which both members of the dyad struggle to keep inner and outer both separate and related.
